title: Vector SDK: Private Bots on Nostr
subtitle: Identity, channels, events, communities, encryption and operations for Vector bots, with Python labs
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: A hands-on course based on the published vector_sdk crate, version 0.12.0 (11 November 2026, MIT, Rust 1.75+), its README, changelog and examples. Older write-ups describe 0.3.0 or 0.2.1; this course follows the current crate. Learn how a Rust bot gets an identity, sends and receives through one Channel API, handles events and history, declares typed slash commands, joins and runs communities with roles, overwrites and moderation policies, uses the optional voice, Mini App, Tor and I2P features, and is secured and troubleshot. Labs run offline and simulate the rules in Python, since Rust cannot run here.

chapters.title: What the Vector SDK is: crate 0.12.0 and its parts

maps.title: Vector SDK 0.12.0
links: Features | add | tor i2p voice whisper xdc

summary: vector_sdk is a Rust crate for building bots and clients for Vector, a private encrypted messenger built on Nostr. Version 0.12.0 was published on 11 November 2026 under the MIT licence, and needs Rust 1.75 or newer.

It sits on top of vector-core, which does the encryption, networking and storage. You write about a dozen lines to get a bot that sends and receives messages, files and reactions, joins communities, and survives network drops.
Older write-ups are out of date. A GitBook page described version 0.3.0 and a standalone repository showed 0.2.1. This course follows the published 0.12.0 crate, its README, changelog and examples.

glossary.def: The Rust crate for building Vector bots; the crate name uses an underscore, the docs.rs name a hyphen.
The engine crate underneath: protocol, encryption, networking and storage. Version 0.11 is required by SDK 0.12.
A Cargo option that compiles in an optional part: tor, i2p, voice, whisper or xdc.
Minimum supported Rust version; 1.75 for this crate.
An open protocol of signed events passed through relays.

keyPoints: cargo add vector_sdk and cargo add tokio --features full.
0.12.0 published 2026-11-11, MIT, MSRV 1.75, edition 2021.
Features: tor, i2p, voice, whisper, xdc. None are on by default.
Depends on vector-core 0.11, nostr-sdk 0.45, tokio 1.49.
Repository: github.com/VectorPrivacy/Vector; docs: docs.rs/vector-sdk.

items: ELI5. A bot is a robot mail carrier for a secret-letter club. The robot's rulebook is a Rust crate, and the newest rulebook is the one to read, because old ones get out of date.

A messenger bot needs three things: an identity, a way to send privately, and a way to hear what happens. The Vector SDK packages all three. You never touch the protocol or the encryption yourself; the crate does it for you.

lesson.code:
# Cargo
cargo add vector_sdk
cargo add tokio --features full

items: This is the crate's own quick start. Notice that the handler receives the bot and the message, skips its own messages with is_mine, and replies. The same code works for direct messages and for community channels.

The crate has no optional parts switched on by default. The tor and i2p features route traffic through anonymity networks, voice and whisper let a bot join voice calls and transcribe speech, and xdc lets it take part in Mini Apps. Each adds dependencies, so enable only what you need.

Versions matter. The library is young and moves quickly, with minor releases adding large features. Pin an exact version in Cargo.toml, read the changelog before upgrading, and treat anything you read elsewhere as possibly out of date.

practice.solution:
def meets_msrv(rust_version):
    parts = rust_version.split('.')
    major = int(parts[0])
    minor = int(parts[1])
    if major != 1:
        return major > 1
    return minor >= 75

    pb = [int(x) for x in b.split('.')]
    return pa > pb

chapters.title: Accounts and keys: identity, data directory, one bot per process

maps.title: Accounts
links: No key | creates | Identity on first run

summary: There are four ways to give the bot an identity. Give no key and build creates one on first run and reuses it every run after. Give an nsec, a twelve word mnemonic, or a password for keys that are encrypted at rest. VectorBot::generate_nsec mints a fresh key yourself.

A keyless bot's identity is stable across restarts, so it keeps its chats and community memberships. Storage defaults to a per-OS application directory. Override it with data_dir or the VECTOR_DATA_DIR variable.
Every bot on a machine needs its own data directory, and a bot owns its process while it runs, so run one bot per process.

glossary.def: A bech32 private key beginning nsec1; whoever has it is the bot.
The matching public key beginning npub1; safe to share.
A twelve word seed phrase from which the key is derived.
Where the bot stores its identity and database.
An environment variable that sets the data directory.

keyPoints: No key: created on first run, reused afterwards.
.nsec(), .mnemonic(), .password(), VectorBot::generate_nsec().
.data_dir(path) or VECTOR_DATA_DIR; one directory per bot.
Run one bot per process; for more bots run more processes.
A bot on Tor or I2P must name it again on every run.

items: ELI5. Your bot has a public name tag anyone can read and a secret code only it knows. The first time it starts, if you give it no code, it makes one and keeps it in its own drawer.

Think of the key as the bot's passport. The npub is the number everyone can read, and the nsec is the secret that proves it is really the bot. Anyone holding the nsec can act as the bot, so it must never appear in code, logs or screenshots.

Leaving the key out is perfect for a first bot. The first run creates an identity and stores it in the data directory, and every later run loads the same one. If you run several keyless bots on one machine, give each its own data directory, or they would share one identity.
A mnemonic is a twelve word seed phrase that can recreate the key. Treat it exactly like an nsec. The password option is only for keys that were saved encrypted.
A bot owns the process while it runs, so the rule is one bot per process. To run several bots, run several processes, each with its own data directory and key.
Read secrets from the environment, as the examples do with VECTOR_NSEC. If you suspect a key leaked, move the bot to a new identity and tell the people who use it the new npub.

chapters.title: Channels: one API for DMs and communities
summary: You send through a Channel. A direct message chat and a community channel are handled identically, so you never branch on which one it is. Get one with bot.channel(id), bot.dm(npub), or msg.channel() on an incoming message.

The channel methods cover send, reply, post with options, react and unreact, typing, edit, delete, send_file and send_bytes. Incoming messages also have reply and react shortcuts, and received files are in msg.message.attachments.
channel.post takes PostOptions so a message can be a reply, can expire after a number of seconds, or can be addressed to one bot.

glossary.def: A conversation you can send to: a DM or a community channel.
Settings for post: reply_to, expires_in, to_bot and caption.
A file received with a message; fetch it with download_attachment or save_attachment.
A pack emoji written as :code: in any message the bot sends.
A short lived signal that the bot is composing.

keyPoints: bot.channel(id).send(text) works for DMs and community channels.
reply(msg_id, text) threads; post(text, PostOptions) adds expiry or addressing.
send_file(path) from disk; send_bytes(bytes, name, opts) from memory.
react, unreact, react_custom; edit and delete only your own messages.
typing() shows the indicator.

items: ELI5. A channel is a door to a chat. Whether the chat is private or a big club room, you push the same buttons: say, answer, smiley, send a file.
The big idea is that a Channel hides the difference between a private chat and a community room. Your code says send, reply or react, and the SDK works out the encryption and the relays.

post is the general sender. With PostOptions you can reply to a message, set an expiry so the message disappears after a number of seconds, address a command to one particular bot, or attach a caption to a file that you send from memory with send_bytes.

Custom emoji work by equipping a pack with bot.subscribe_emoji_pack, then writing :code: in text. If two packs share a shortcode with different images, the SDK numbers them, such as :love~1: and :love~2:.

A bot can only edit and delete its own messages. To remove someone else's message in a community it needs moderation rights, covered later. Remember that everything the bot posts in a community is visible to everyone who can read that channel.

chapters.title: Receiving: handlers, BotEvent and history
summary: bot.on_message handles every incoming chat message. bot.on_event gives the full BotEvent stream, and bot.run does the same but also exits cleanly on Ctrl-C. A slow handler will not hold up the others.

BotEvent covers Ready, Message, Reaction, ReactionRemoved, Edit, Delete, MemberJoin, MemberLeave, Typing, CommunityChange, Dissolved, VoicePresence, Invite, Removed and more, each naming what changed and, where it applies, who did it.
Everything sent since the bot began listening arrives once, live or through a catch-up. What came earlier is history. Read it on purpose with channel.history.

glossary.def: The enum of everything the bot can be told about.
Fires once per listen when the realtime subscriptions are registered.
One event per change to roles, channels, bans, timeouts, pins and more, naming who made it.
Messages from before the bot began listening; read explicitly, never pushed as events.
A durable position (time and id) used to page through history.

keyPoints: on_message for chat; on_event or run for everything.
Skip msg.is_mine() to avoid reply loops.
Ready fires even with zero communities.
News arrives once; old messages are history, read with channel.history(n).
The bot reconnects and catches up by itself.

items: ELI5. Events are doorbells. Each kind of bell goes to a helper. The bot only hears new bells that rang while it was listening. Older news is in the diary, which you read on purpose.

A bot is driven by events, like a switchboard. The SDK turns each thing that happens into a BotEvent, and your handler decides what to do. Handlers run independently, so one slow handler does not stall the others.

The first arm skips the bot's own messages. The second welcomes someone who joined. The third notices when a moderator deleted a message, which a plain message handler would never see. The last arm ignores everything else, so adding new variants later does not break your code.

The SDK is careful about what counts as news. Anything sent after the bot began listening arrives exactly once, even if the bot was reconnecting. A relay replaying a month-old join does not greet anyone, and old messages pulled in by a sync never show up as Message events.

To read earlier messages, ask for them: channel.history(n) returns the newest n messages the bot holds locally, and history_before takes a Cursor to page further back. A Cursor is a time and an id, so it stays valid even if its message is later deleted.

Typing events carry an until time, the moment the indicator expires, so a bot can ignore stale ones. Keep the process alive after registering handlers: if main returns, the bot stops hearing anything.

chapters.title: Slash commands with typed arguments

maps.title: Commands
links: Manifest | is published | At listen start

summary: Do not parse message text by hand. Declare a command with bot.command(name, description), add typed arguments, and give it a handler. The SDK publishes a manifest, so every Vector client shows a slash picker with a field per argument.

Argument types are string, int, number, flag, user and choice. A choice becomes a dropdown, a user becomes a member picker, and an int becomes a number field. The client validates the input before it is sent.
A matched command runs its handler and never reaches on_message, so commands and free chat can live side by side.

glossary.def: The published list of a bot's commands and their arguments.
The object a command handler receives, with typed getters and reply.
An argument limited to a fixed list of options, shown as a dropdown.
Whether the user must supply the argument.
A matched command is handled by its own function and not passed on to message handlers.

keyPoints: bot.command(name, description).string(...).choice(...).run(handler).
Types: string, int, number, flag, user, choice.
Read values with ctx.str, ctx.int, ctx.number, ctx.flag.
Matched commands never reach on_message.
The wire format is plain text like '/roll 20', so old clients can type it.

items: ELI5. A slash command is a form with blanks that every phone draws for you. The bot only receives neat, checked answers instead of messy typing.

Parsing chat text yourself is fragile: people mistype, add spaces, and forget options. Declared commands move that work into the client, which draws a form and checks it, so your handler only ever sees well-formed values.

The third argument of each declaration says whether it is required. The choice call takes the list of allowed values, so a user cannot send an unit you do not handle. Read values off the context by name, and supply a default for optional ones.

The manifest is published automatically when the bot starts listening, and its order is the order you registered the commands, so the picker stays stable across restarts. There is a limit on the number of commands, and names must be unique.
On the wire a command is just message text such as slash roll 20, parsed against the manifest. That means any client, however old, can invoke a command by typing it, and your bot can still serve it.
Because matched commands are consumed, do not also expect them in on_message. Keep free-form chat handling there, and keep commands for actions with clear arguments.

chapters.title: Communities: joining, members and invites
summary: A community is a shared space with members, roles and channels. Your bot can join one by link with bot.join, preview a link first with bot.preview_link, or create its own with bot.create_community.

Invites are handled by the invite policy on the builder. Manual is the default: invites wait for bot.pending_invites and bot.accept_invite. Public accepts from anyone. Whitelist accepts only listed npubs and ignores the rest. Auto-accept also picks up invites that arrived while the bot was offline.
When a message arrives from a community, msg.member() gives the sender as a member you can act on: kick, ban, unban, grant or revoke admin, and check is_admin.

glossary.def: Manual, Public or Whitelist; decides what happens to invitations.
An invitation waiting for a manual decision.
Reading a link's details before joining; says whether it was read from the community itself (verified).
A person in a community, with actions such as kick and ban.
Only these npubs may invite the bot; entries are bech32 npub1 values.

keyPoints: Builder: .public() or .whitelist([...]); default is Manual.
Manual: bot.pending_invites() then bot.accept_invite(id).
bot.join(link), bot.preview_link(link), bot.create_community(name, NewCommunity).
msg.member(): kick(), ban(), unban(), grant_admin(), revoke_admin(), is_admin().
Auto-accept also joins invites that arrived while offline.

items: ELI5. A club sends your bot invitations. It can say yes to all, yes only to friends on a list, or ask a grown-up each time.

Think of a clubhouse that sends your bot invitations. Manual means a person checks each one. Public means the bot joins any club that asks. Whitelist means it only joins clubs invited by people on its list, which keeps it from being spammed into random communities.

With a whitelist, an invite from anyone else is ignored. The list must hold bech32 npub values, and the builder converts hex keys for you. A restarted bot still joins invites that arrived while it was down, in the automatic modes.

Moderation actions are checked the way every member's client would judge them. If the bot lacks the right, the call returns an error instead of publishing an edit that everyone would ignore, so handle the error rather than assuming success.

Racing bans compose: when many ban calls happen at once during a spam wave, they queue per community and drain into one change. For a whole wave, ban_many and unban_many batch the work into a single key rotation.

chapters.title: Running a community: roles, channels, permissions and policies
summary: From 0.12 a bot can do what a person with admin rights can do: create roles with permissions, make categories and channels, set per-channel overwrites, time members out, set nicknames, pin messages, and read a typed audit log.
Each action is checked the way every member's client will judge it, so a refusal comes back as an error rather than an edit that everyone ignores.
Moderation policies add rulebooks. community.policies() writes rules such as words, links, repetition, flooding or a joining cohort, previews them against real history, and acts only when armed.

glossary.def: A named set of permissions given to members; created with RoleSpec.
Bit flags such as KICK, BAN, MODERATE_MEMBERS, VIEW_CHANNEL and SEND_MESSAGES, combined with the | operator.
A channel level rule that allows or denies permissions for a role or member.
A temporary silence applied to a member for a duration.
A policy autopilot acts on verdicts only after arm; until then it is a dry run.

create_category, create_channel_with(NewChannel::default().private().in_category(id)).
channel.set_overwrite(Overwrite::role(&role).allow(...)).
member.timeout(duration), member.add_role(&role), msg.pin().
Policies start in dry-run; only arm() lets them act, and never on less than proof.

items: ELI5. Running a club means giving out badges (roles), making rooms, and putting people in time-out. A careful helper rehearses first and only acts when it has proof.

Running a community is mostly bookkeeping: who may do what, and where. Roles bundle permissions, categories group channels, and overwrites adjust the rules for one channel. The SDK exposes each as a typed call.
Permissions are bit flags, so combining them uses the bitwise or operator and testing one uses a bitwise and. member.can and channel.permissions_of let a bot check what someone may do before it acts.

The audit log is typed. Each entry has an action, a target and an actor, so a bot can answer questions like who changed this role. BotEvent::CommunityChange pushes the same facts live, naming who made each change.

Policies are the careful way to moderate automatically. You write named rules, preview them against recent history, then enable them. A verdict says whether it can be proved from the record or is only inference, and a strong hunch lands in a queue for a human instead of triggering an action.

An autopilot starts as a dry run that only reports what it would do. Calling arm makes it act, and it still never removes anyone on less than proof. Keep a person in the loop for anything destructive, such as dissolving a community.

chapters.title: Voice, Mini Apps and the optional networks

maps.title: Optional features
links: Cargo feature | plus builder | Both needed

summary: Four optional features extend a bot. Voice joins voice channels and hears 48 kHz mono audio per speaker. Whisper turns clips into text. Xdc joins Mini Apps, small shared apps in a chat. Tor and I2P route traffic through anonymity networks.
Tor and I2P need the Cargo feature and a builder call, .tor() or .i2p(). The feature alone only compiles the code in. A bot on Tor or I2P must name it on every run.
For web requests, such as to a language model, use vector_sdk::net::build_http_client so a bot on Tor or I2P never leaks its address with a side request.

glossary.def: A channel where members talk; the bot gets PCM audio per speaker.
A 20 ms block of 48 kHz mono audio.
A .xdc file shared in a chat: a game or tool everyone who opens it uses together.
A bot's connection to one open copy of a Mini App.
A gateway from I2P to the ordinary internet.

keyPoints: Voice: channel.join_voice(); call.listen(); call.say(pcm).
Audio is 48 kHz mono PCM; a frame is 20 ms.
Mini Apps: bot.xdc(app_id).run(handler); sessions end after 3 minutes idle or 15 minutes quiet.
Tor and I2P need the feature and .tor() or .i2p().
Use vector_sdk::net::build_http_client for side requests.

items: ELI5. Extra gadgets: a phone line for voices, a game table for little apps, and secret tunnels for hiding where you are. Each gadget has to be switched on in two places.

Voice turns a bot into a participant in a call. Audio arrives as short frames, twenty milliseconds each, one stream per speaker. At 48 thousand samples per second, one frame is 960 samples. The bot can queue its own audio with say, and wait for it with say_and_wait.

A bot must be listening, through run or on_event, to join a call. A call ends when a moderator disconnects or moves the bot: listen returns None and say returns false, and moved_to names the new channel if you want to follow. Building voice needs cmake for libopus.

A Mini App is a web app packaged as an xdc file. With the xdc feature the bot can be an opponent, a referee, or the server behind an app that needs more than a phone. Handler sessions end when the handler returns, after 3 minutes with nobody connected, or after 15 minutes without a message.
Be aware of what Mini Apps reveal. Players in a session can see each other's IP address, and the bot's. A bot on Tor or I2P stays out of sessions unless you explicitly allow outside transport.

chapters.title: Security, privacy and troubleshooting

maps.title: Operations
links: Not connected | means | build not done

summary: Treat the nsec and mnemonic as passwords: read them from the environment or a secret store, never commit or log them, and rotate when in doubt. Use wss relays, cap the size of files you accept, and keep logs free of message text.

Be honest about limits. Relays can see metadata and can delay or withhold messages, profile information is public, and a leaked key can expose what that key could read. Voice and Mini App sessions can reveal network addresses unless the bot uses Tor or I2P.
Most failures are simple: using the bot before build finishes, letting the process exit, a relative file path, or missing rights. vector-lab can test a setup against real relays before you deploy.

glossary.def: A websocket secured with TLS.
Facts about a message such as time and size that remain visible even when the content is encrypted.
A tool in the repository that runs bots against real relays and checks what each saw.
A process manager such as systemd that restarts the bot.
Written steps for operating and recovering a service.

keyPoints: Never hardcode, commit or log keys.
Await build() before any other call.
No events: keep the process alive.
Relative file paths follow the working directory; use absolute paths in services.
Test against real relays with vector-lab before deploying.

items: ELI5. Keep the secret code in a locked drawer, check the cheap things first when a toy breaks, and test with pretend friends before the real party.
Security for a bot is mostly discipline. The encryption is the SDK's job, but the key, the host and the logs are yours. A bot that logs every message has undone the privacy it was built to provide.

Keep keys out of code and out of version control. Read VECTOR_NSEC from the environment, give the data directory restrictive file permissions, and keep a plan for rotating the identity if it leaks. Rotating means a new npub, so tell the people who rely on it.

lesson.code:
# turn on library logging while diagnosing (set RUST_LOG for Rust crates)
RUST_LOG=vector_sdk=debug cargo run --example echo_bot

# check a setup against real relays
cargo run -p vector-lab -- all --relays wss://your.relay

items: When something fails, check the cheap things first. Is the process running? Did build finish before the first call? Is the key right? Does the bot have the right in that community? Is the relay reachable? Only then read deeper logs.

Two classic mistakes: registering handlers and then letting main return, and relying on a relative path in a service. A service started by systemd runs from a different folder than your shell, so send_file with a relative name may not find the file.

For retries, wait longer each time with a cap, and treat errors differently. A network error deserves a retry, a bad key does not. The SDK already reconnects and catches up for you, so do not add a second reconnect loop on top.

practice.title: Backoff with cap
practice.intro: Write waits(n, base, cap): return the first n retry waits; the first is base, each next doubles, never above cap.
practice.solution:
def waits(n, base, cap):
    out = []
    w = base
    for i in range(n):
        out.append(min(w, cap))
        w = w * 2
    return out
